Prologue The first age of man ended much as it had begun :  with silence.  At the close of the 22 nd  century, Earth stood empty, bereft of humans, void of their monuments.  B easts once again ruled the planet. The instrument of man's demise, the alien weapon found beneath the ice, now stood as the last  temple  to technology on the small blue world.  Though Earth stood empty of man, the universe did not. Seeing the end coming, humanity, in a last desperate act to save itself, created the ARC.  With the advanced knowledge gleaned from the alien weapon, humankind now could safely enter a frozen state of slumber and awaken centuries later. The last remnants of humanity, twenty thousand souls in all, slept away the ages aboard the massive ship as it floated out near  M ars until it was safe to step foot upon the globe once again. The grand ARC, man's best hope for a future, eventually returned to the little blue planet, the last evidence of man's mastery over the machine. The ship's artificial intelligence watched and waited, standing vigil, analyzing and scanning the world man once called home. Only once the world was again deemed safe were the PODS release d  back to the now-feral world,  the slumbering inheritors of man's destiny .  Frozen in the small pods, they would rocket back to the planet, allowing  man  once again to take their rightful place upon the Earth.  However, some did not return. Either by accident or  by  some purpose not understood by man or machine,  their PODS  floated above the planet, locked in orbit  and  in sleep, randomly falling to the world as ages pas sed .  Those who paid attention to  such things called them fallen .  H ere is the story of  one  lost soul, robbed of his world and returned to  an  E arth which regressed to a time long before  his own . ONE M A R C U S Honor is the first of the four tenants.  It is the measure by which all men are judged. -Book of  Artus  “Am I home?”  H is voice still suffering the effects of the chemicals  used in reanimat ion ,  Marcus’s  mouth uttering a  scratchy low whisper . He  sound ed  more like an old man of one hundred  rather than the spry  twenty-seven  he was.   He   paused  in  surprise .   T hat isn’t my voice ,  is it ?   Marcus blinked  back  fresh tears as  sunlight   seared   retinas  that had not felt the light for a  millennium . H is vision  slowly  came  back into focus, fuzzy blobs of color sharpening into  the  technicolor  of   early  autumn  leaves . L ooking up ,  he surveyed the  gold and green   canvas  splayed   across the canopy ’s underbelly ,   a  sound like  dry parchment  echoing  through the  trees   as  branches  swayed  in  time to the rising  breeze .  Earth . He heaved  a relieved sigh ,   beginning  to  relax,   fear dissipating  to be  replaced with  familiarity .  J oints that had not been  used  in centuries  complained   as he willed his body to move . Turning ,  he studied the remnants of the silver ,  teardrop - shaped craft  half - buried at the end of a long ravine created when it hit the ground.  How long have I been away?   He looked  to the surrounding fauna for answers, but none came.  Marcus winced as his muscles protested  with  pain, testing his strength. The  one-piece   G ortex   outfit he wore stretching with the movements of his body, the restriction of the outfit causing him to scowl in annoyance.  Here I am ,  he  thought,  a smile replacing the annoyed wince as he studied the lush  forest  before him.  Marcus had spent time in forests, mostly training with the Army, but it had not been a place he  ever  felt at home. In  fact,  during his time with the Army Corp of Engineers ,  he spent most of his time in the deserts of Africa, engineering irrigation solutions for remote areas. The forest ,  though familiar ,  was not the comfort he had hoped it would be.  He continued to sit for a moment, not trusting his muscles to stand . H e missed the desert, missed the work he had been good at it . I t had been his reputation  for  solving unsolvable problems that brought him to the attention of the ARC project.  Marcus shook his head as memories flooded his mind . T he machine found in the ice, the discovery of its purpose as a weapon ,  and then the panic .   The ARC project had been formed as a  last-ditch  effort . T hey had studied the machine, learned from it ,  and then applied some of that technology to allow mankind the ability to launch  into space and sleep away centuries as it waited for the  planet  to heal.  “Here I am , ” he said again , out loud this time,   using  that  gravelly voice  which was  damn near unrecognizable to him. He shook it off as he unsteadily got to his feet. Shuffling over to the ship ,  he leaned down and studied the damage to the hull .  I t isn’t going to fly again .   F or a moment ,  he looked up  and  imagined he could see the large mothership that hovered in  geosynchronous  orbit,  PODS   lined up in docks as they waited for the Artificial Intelligence to deem the planet safe and begin  the  launch sequence. He had  spent  centuries on board that ship,  frozen in  sleep, waiting for the computer to finally launch him and all his fellow volunteers back to the planet that  had  birthed humanity.  Turning with a start as something large moved through the woods some distance away, he felt fear creep up his back and shambled his way towards the rear of the  teardrop - shaped ship. He might have been trained as a soldier, but Marcus Gavin had spent his career building and creating, not fighting . W hat few combat skills he had were remnants of the  basic  training he had once received.  Reaching the back of the small vessel ,  he breathed a sigh  of   relief to see that the section had been undamaged.  He  listened for another tell-tale sign of the large creature in the woods, but none came . F eeling  around the surface of the vessel ,  he found the small indent he had been looking for and pushed . A  recessed keyboard slid smoothly from the  ship . After t apping  in a  code,  he   waited   for what seemed like an eternity  as a door slid  open,  revealing a  packed storage compartment. Marcus  began pulling out  t he gear stored there, mostly emergency  supplies should he find himself far from civilization :  a backpack, a  tent,  food ,  and stored water ,  all of which he stacked neatly next to the ship.  Reaching  in again,  Marcus smiled as his hand closed over a large black plastic case.  He  opened it to reveal a Military issue carbine and pistol, complete with extra clips stored  nea tl y  in the padded case.  Plucking the  rifle,  a magazine ,  and a handful of rounds  from the case ,  he quickly pushed a few rounds into the clip and slapped it home  with a reassuring  clank , the  metal-on-metal  sound of a bullet being chambered comforting as he moved around the ship  and faced  the direction of the sound.  After some deliberation,  he  pointed  the rifle at a large tree and aimed, squeezing the trigger  to let loose a warning shot.   Depressing  the  trigger,  he tensed for the recoil of the small bullpup  and was rewarded with a hollow click .  Marcus pulled  his cheek  from  the stock,  studying  the weapon curiously .   H e ejected the round and chambered another, squeezing the trigger . O nce again  came the metallic click . “What the hell ? ” he whispered. His voice sound ed  at least  semi - normal ,  he thought distractedly.  Pulling the  magazine,  he popped a round out and proceeded to rummage around in the overloaded pack until he came out with a small  tool case . Carefully ,  he removed the round from the shell and upend ed  the metal casing . A fter a few hard taps ,   a small  solid  clump of yellowish rock tumbled out of the bullet casing. “Of all the stupid … ”  He  closed  his eyes to swallow down the panic starting to build in his chest .   E xpired . He  wanted  to either laugh or cry ;   he wasn’t sure which .  Apparently,  no one had sufficiently solved the problem of  bullets a few centuries old . He stared in disbelief at the solid chunk of cordite in his hand. How is this even possible ? Marcus thought, pushing his thumb against the solid mass and with a medium push broke the  chunk into smaller pieces the century old gun powder was useless . Having been preserved in zero G, should have protected it. Yet for some reason it had not, a few minutes  later ,  Marcus had open and inspected five more roun ds all with the same result.  T he guns were useless ,  he  realized . R eturning the carbine to the black case ,  he began searching the equipment for anything else he could use  as a weapon . Within twenty minutes ,  he had laid out an Ontario K-Bar knife and a survival hatche t .  Shaking his head,  he picked up the knife and weighed it in his hand . I f  whatever is out there is  as big as it sounds, this is just going to piss it off ,   but hell ,   it’s  better than nothing .  Marcus had  always  managed to find  and implement  solution s ,  much to the amazement of his superiors and his peers.   This singular talent had gained him rank, success and a place on the project,  Now the talented problem-solver   scanned the surrounding trees , his mind working a mile a minute as he put his intellect to the problem of survival .  Picking  up the hatche t  he swung it  w ith a few sure  str o kes ,  coming  away with a long ,  straight branch .  H e quickly took the edge of the hatchet over  one end of  the staff, sharpening the edge  to a point .  After  testing the sharpness of the point with his thumb Marcus set the newly created spear aside. *** Marcus removed  the wet ,  chemical - covered ,   one - piece outfit ,   he rummaged through one of the cases until he produced a set of military battle dress, socks ,  a few t-shirts ,  and some fresh underwear .  H e worked slowly, doing  his best to wipe away the chemicals that covered his body head to  toe , the mixture that had assisted in his cryogenic sleep now merely an annoyance,  It was thick and sticky,  but had done the job of protecting his body and keeping him alive during the long sleep,  Once he had removed as much of the muck as he could , he dressed ,  wincing at the  way the clothing caught on his still sticky skin .  After donning fresh clothes, he realized the routine had mitigated a lot of the agitation and stress  of the morning, taking a moment he sucked   in an   appreciative breath of the clean forest air . H e had  sat through detailed briefings   of  the potential devastation the weapon  c ould have wrought  upon the planet . H e could have returned to a desert, or worse ,  a planet barren of all life . H e  was pleased to see the surrounding woods untouched by what they  once  thought would be the end of the planet.  The machine was ancient when they pulled it from the ice of the arctic . I t was a mystery,   and  for fifty years ,  it sat dormant at a research facility . T he scientists in charge of studying it had not known what it was they had  until,   during an experiment ,   the machine suddenly  activated. It had taken another year to finally figure out what it was that they had turned  on,  and  more  importantly ,  how to read the countdown that had begun on that fateful day.  T hey had lost a year out of six, leaving five years before the machine would destroy mankind  by  releasing virulent pathogens and nanite armies to remove humans and  their  creations. Shortly thereafter ,  the ARC project was started . T aking technology learned from the machine, they began to build ships, technologies ,  and the process of placing humans in Cryonic sleep, freezing them until  the onboard AI determined it save to return.  There should be more . M ore pods, more people . But  looking around , he saw  no sign  to suggest he wasn’t alone . He needed information .  He again reached  into the pod ,  and from the center of the control system , he  removed a metallic object that looked like a chrome egg — another piece of that altered technology . P lacing the small device on the ground ,  it began to pulse red. Standing and watching it, he waited as the red lights turned yellow and then solid green . O nce it had made its connection with the mothership above, the small egg  began to  rise   off the ground, coming to float at eye level .  A s Marcus watched ,  a person began to form around the device ,  first as a wireframe and then filling out as the  holographic  projectors  within  activated, eventually leaving a dark silver silhouette standing in front of him. “Sentinel is online .  Marcus Gavin, by your command , ” the soft female voice stated .   H e sighed . A t least the VI worked . I t was a simple virtual interface without intelligence of its own ;  the device would connect to the ship, allowing the  a rtificial  i ntelligence there to interact with a  human . L ike a puppet for the AI, it  gave  him an interface to communicate with the ship — and hopefully other volunteers .  “Sentinel, please review  the  mission and bring me up to speed on the current situation , ” he stated clearly . H e watched the silhouette  freeze  for a minute, the device communicating and receiving information from the ship  still circling  E arth .  Finally,  the VI  nodded  its head .  “Certainly ,  Marcus , ” it  began,  and the image of the person vanished ,  forming instead into an image of the planet hanging in front of him. He knew it was from the  ship’s  archives, the image centuries old, but still ,  seeing Earth and all its lights and people from space caused his breath to pause . I t was his home .  “Beginning  time - lapse of events , ” Sentinel  s tated ,  and a fter a moment ,   the  AI sped up the image of   E arth’s rotation .  Marcus watched ships launch from the surface and quickly load into the mothership . T hat had been the pods ;  they had loaded everyone into them on  E arth ,  and then like cargo ,  shipped the frozen volunteers to the mothership ’s  berths.  The flurry of activity  stopped,  and the  E arth continued to spin, the rotation speeding up even more . T o Marcus’s horror ,  the lights on the planet began to go out, slow at first and then faster and faster . B efore long ,  the planet was dark, a red mist  crawl ing  over the surface, reminding Marcus of a colony of ants . E ach  continent disappeared,   and  the planet  was  covered  in a red haze . H e didn’t know what it was but decided to wait to ask, allowing the visual briefing to continue . E ventually ,  the red haze faded as the planet spun, faster and faster.  For almost thirty minutes ,   Marcus stared in rapt fascination as the  planet  spun  at incredible speeds, the surface a blue blur  until instantly ,  it slowed ,  and as Marcus watched, pods exploded from the mothership and began to descend to  E arth . H e watched a second ,  and then a third mothership came into view ,  and those two launched  their  pods, the small metal ships descending to  the surface.   T he planet sped up again, slowing  once in a while  as a random pod launched, then it would speed up again ,  repeating the process twelve times, until a final pod  launched,  and the visual briefing stopped.  Marcus stood there silent as he thought through what he just witnessed .   S omething is wrong . “Sentinel, what can you tell me about the red dust that was released over the planet ? ” he  asked  and waited as the  E arth ’s image  dissolved and  the  VI’s  human representation  reappeared  in front of him.  “From our sensors,  we believe it  was a  swarm  of nanite machines . I ts purpose was to deconstruct any artificial  material  on the planet . O nce done ,  the swarm eventually died . H owever ,  our  scans  indicate  that  as they cleared the planet, they  left   large  crystal  formations  covering  the  surface. T hese formations pulse with a frequency that has since interfered with our ability to document and record from the planet surface. ”   Marcus looked  around  and  finally  noticed small crystal growths on the trees and ground, the red,  blue,  and green spires seeming to grow on anything. He  bent  down to study  one.  It looked harmless . He r each ed  out  to touch  it with his finger,  and  just as quickly ,  he pulled it away as if the rock had bit ten  him . S lowly ,  Marcus reached out again and touched the rock . I t thrummed as if power was coursing through  it;  he could feel the vibration into his fingers and hand .  After a moment ,  he pulled his hand away .  H e tried to count how many crystals he could see  around him ,  but  Marcus quickly lost count at a thousand . A lmost every tree had at least one .  A n invasive species .   He shook  his head  and  turned back to the VI .  “ Are the crystals some kind of generator or communication  equipment? ”  “ Yes  to both questions . T here is a sort of power emanating  through  them ,  but the source is unknown ,  and they are operating on a wavelength  that sends  out low - level communications, though it is too low to reach orbit and only seems effective up to a thousand feet from the crystal itself . T he signal is constant ,  so it is more of a simple hum  th a n  anything intelligent . A lso ,  you will notice the crystals are no longer giant spire s. A  few centuries ’  time has broken them down . W hat is left  is in the soil   and  has become  part of the ecosystem . T he crystals seem to be benign and coexist with the environment .”   Marcus shook his head ,  looking back to the crystal . T hat was an interesting mystery, but one outside of his expertise. “ Sentinel ,  why launch random pods after the initial exodus?” he asked, remembering the lone pods launched over time.  “Due to a  malfunction,  over thirty pods remained on the ship  while  they were repaired . T hey were then launched and returned to earth . A s of this time ,  twelve of the thirty have been returned over a period of three centuries . ”  Marcus  couldn’t believe  what he had just heard  “Sentinel, what is the reason for the timeframe ?   S urely it has not taken that long to fix twelve pods?” he  asked . S omething wasn’t  right,  but this was a machine, not made to be malicious or nefarious . That only reassured him a little. The VI paused  to communicate with the mothership , this time longer  than  normal . W hen it came back ,  the silhouette shrugged in  such a  human manner ,  Marcus almost  took  a step back.  “That is unknown . T he answer to that question is not available beyond  administration - level access , ” Sentinel  stated,  and Marcus narrowed his eyes .  S ince when did a repair get  top - level access  only ?   “Sentinel, who authorized the change in security for the repair information?” he asked and again waited for the machine’s answer .   “That information is not available beyond  administration - level access , ” the machine stated.  Marcus shook his head . S omething about that wasn’t ,  right but he had much more  pressing issues . H e mentally prepared himself and then asked the  most important  question .  “Sentinel, I assume the last pod to return was mine . W hat is the timeframe from the  original  exodus to my pod returning to the planet ? ”  He   k new well he wouldn’t like the answer.  After a moment ,  Sentinel came back .  “Two hundred twelve years since  the  exodus , ” she  said,  and it felt as if  he had been kicked in the gut .  P lacing his hands on  the  knees , Marcus  tried to get control of the looming panic that threatened to overtake him .  Two hundred years . P eople have been on the planet for two centuries .  W hat the hell happened ?  More importantly, why had no one come to welcome him ?  T hinking  through his options ,  he queried Sentinel again. “Sentinel, can you scan the surrounding area for populations, civilization s,  or communication of any kind ?  Find  a concentration of people . ”  Sentinel  paused to interface with the ship and  returned quicker  than  he expected .  “Marcus ,  because of the interference  from the crystals , I am unable to lock on to  any location of a human population . H owever ,  I can tell you that there are no communications either over this location or  across  the entire North American continent . N o  digital  or analog broadcasts have been detected since the exodus . ”  The small ember of hope that had sprouted in his chest died.  How can that be ?   P eople  had  been back for two hundred years . W ith the supplies and expertise of twenty thousand people returned, surely there  should have been  some sort of civilization . A gain ,  he closed his eyes, the weight of the information threatening to crush him as he battled to keep the panic at bay .  Were  there still people  left?   C ould the effects of the machine have lasted  and killed the first to return?   That’s not helpful .  H e needed a plan . H e couldn’t stay out here in the woods waiting for someone to come and get him. He was no survivalist ;  he was a damn engineer . M aybe he should have gone to ranger school when he had the chan c e.  After a few minutes of pacing ,  he had not come up with anything that could even be considered a plan. With a sigh ,  he turned back to the VI .  “Sentinel, based on the current information ,  do you have a suggestion for a course of action that will allow me to possibly reconnect with the population on the planet , ” he asked ,  and with a mental wince,  he  waited for the answer.  A moment later ,  the VI nodded .  “ B ased on the limited information we  have ,  it is my suggestion that  your  first stop  sh ould be the supply bunkers . Y ou have limited supplies ,  and since it could  take  some time to  locate  others, you will need to ensure your ability to survive , ”  t he VI stated calmly ,  and Marcus could have slapped himself on the forehead.  “Of  c ourse , ”  h e  mumbled .  “ The damn bunkers . ”   D uring the planning phase of the project, the ARC leaders had set about building bunkers throughout the  north western  U nited  S tates, where the volunteers would later land to rebuild . K nowing the ships  couldn’t  carry the supplies and  that  the status of the planet would be unknown,  the  bunkers were created to ensure that equipment, supplies ,  and food would be available to the volunteers upon  their  return.  Marcus knew it was a long shot . H e was  ten   centuries late to the party,  and  it was very possible that those bunkers would be empty . B ut maybe there would be a clue as to where the volunteers had done. Either way ,  it was a good idea  and worth a shot.  “Sentinel, prepare to guide me to the close st  bunker , ” Marcus  commanded and began to collect his supplies.  *** As the  sun began to descend over the canopy, bringing dusk to the forest, Marcus dropped  his  pack with a grunt .  Sentinel walked over to  a nearby  tree, waiting for orders as he collapsed upon the pack and eyed the VI . H e knew it didn’t really walk ;  the device simply floating  and  gave the appearance its hologram was walking with him.  For the entire day ,  he had followed the damn VI as they navigated the forest westward toward the closest bunker to his ship ’ s landing site. He had covered the ship with dead branches, doing his best to hide it . H e wasn’t sure from what or whom, but it seemed like a good idea at the time . T he exertion of doing that on top of walking made him rethink his earlier decision.  “Sentinel, when will we reach the bunker ? ” he asked, playing his own little game of ‘are we there yet’ with the machine.  “We will reach the bunker tomorrow at noon based on our progress . ”  W ith a grunt, Marcus nodded . He  remove d   his  tent  from his pack  and  set to work. After  clumsily setting up his camp and finally getting a fire started, he  heated  a small can  of   freeze - dried  corn ed  beef hash  using  some of  the precious bottled water  to reconstitute the food . T he result look ed  more like vomit th a n food .  A  rustling from the trees caught his attention. Standing ,  he pulled  out his  hatchet and scanned the canopy as more branches shivered with movement.  Something is up there. He almost jumped out of his skin when a black tendril broke free of the  densely  covered branch and took off across the expanse toward another tree, stopping halfway and simply  hovering, waiting  for something.  Marcus stood there, his jaw agape and the hatchet forgotten ,  as he studied the creature now fully displayed in the waning sunlight of the day.  “Sentinel, can you scan that creature ? ” he whispered and waited as the VI put its palm  up, virtual  windows appearing as the device began to scan the area.  Marcus’s eyes followed  the black scaly body, which measured about six feet in length, ending at a narrow  snake’s  head . But  that wasn’t what bothered him . He focused  on the  bat - like  wings sprouting from halfway  down  its body, the membranous  appendages  lazily flapping as they cupped the  air,  keeping the animal  afloat . “What the hell ? ” he breathed,  un able to take his eyes from the creature.  “Marcus, it appears to be  some kind of hybrid  animal . I t is not the only one of its kind close by .  I would say from the number that this is not a fluke but a mutation in the animal — one that has evolved to become the species , ” Sentinel stated loud enough to startle the creature and send it flying into the far  tree line . J ust as quickly ,  about ten more erupted from the first tree and joined it.  “Well ,  it seems some things have changed since my last time here , ” he said ,  half astonished and half smiling at his weak joke.  *** The next day ,  as the sun finished its climb to  mid-day ,  Marcus found himself standing at the base of a large hill, the churned earth having settled long ago from the looks of it .  “Where are we ,  Sentinel?” he asked ,  looking  around  for signs of the large warehouse - like bunker that should  have been there .  For a few moments ,  the VI stood stalwart before moving again toward the large mound  of dirt .  “The bunker is directly in front of us based on the coordinates in the system .  However,  all scans show that it has been removed from beneath the earth, possibly by the same nanite infestation that removed  all artificial material on the planet .”   Marcus scrambled to  Sentinel .  H e struggled to climb the simple slope ,  a headache that had plagued him all morning getting worse . A  hum had started early that morning ,  and the more they walked ,  the worse it had gotten . H ere at the base of the hill ,  it almost felt as if his entire cranium were vibrating.  When he finally made it  to the top ,  he  looked  over the expanse and marveled at the large hole filled to the brim with crystal spires  of  all colors and all sizes . T he spires reach ed  from the deep pit toward the sky as if someone had lined the entire thing with spikes to kill a giant .  T he nanites converted the supplies , everything— hell ,  the bunker itself — into damn crystals .  “This is not possible . A ccording to my coordinates ,  this is the location of the closest bunker ,  Marcus , ” Sentinel stated, her palm outstretched  to gather  readings from the enormous collection of crystals.  He didn’t need the scans to know what had happened . He slumped  on the edge  in defeat,  rubbing his head as the thrumming  grew   worse ,   squinting down into the large hole of colorful rocks .   W hat the hell is that ?  After a moment ,  he slid down the side of the hill and walked a small distance from the crater - sized hole . T he further he  got  from the collection of crystals ,  the quieter his head  grew .  Finally ,  once he had reached a distance where he could begin to think ,  Marcus began to pace . H e was a problem solver ;  his abilities relied  on  recognizing patterns others missed ,  and something in the back of his mind was going off.  Sentinel had said  something about the crystals and power . S omething about a signal . T hat might explain the feeling in his head . Maybe he  could sense the power or the signal,  similar to   people  who were able to sense.  He was  side - tracking himself ,  and  he  knew it . T hat wasn’t what was bothering him.  P ausing in  mid - pace, he turned to the VI image .  “Sentinel, didn’t you say that the crystals appeared after the dissipation of the red nanite swarm?” he asked, knowing there was a correlation there . P ulling on the thread of thought, he tried to follow it to its conclusion.  After a  moment ary  pause ,  the VI  replie d.   “Yes ,  Marcus, why do you ask?”  W ith a simple nod ,  he continued to pace,  confirming his initial theory.   “ Sentinel ,  scan the makeup of the crystals in that crater and then match it to the known chemical components of what would have been in that bunker . ”  He  cross ed  his fingers that he was wrong. It took almost fifteen minutes before the VI returned .   “It was not easy, the crystals themselves making remote scanning next to impossible, but this unit was able to collect enough local data to do an extrapolation .  According to the scan, the chemical makeup of the crystal collection matches that of the makeup of the building and supplies within the bunker at  eighty - seven percent. ”   Blowing out a breath ,  he eyed the  crystal growths on the  trees around him . He  finally  knew  what he was looking at, what those beautiful monoliths represented.  “Sentinel, I think we are looking at what was left of  the human race — the components of every building, monument, food wrapper ,  and who knows what else that the swarm destroyed .  I think these crystals are the tombstone to our race . ”  Sentinel did not respond,  simpl y   stood there waiting for the next order, despite the  epiphany  that Marcus had just laid on them both.  Suddenly ,  he  was exhausted , drained of whatever energy  had  remained in him . S itting down ,  he hung his head, thinking of all that had been taken from this world, taken from him ,  as he continued to stare at the  innocent - looking crystal s .  As he sat there, a movement caught his eye . T o his left ,  he watched as a small  number  of crystal spires began to move  across  the forest floor . H e  couldn’t  believe i t.   Is  it possible the crystals themselves  are  alive ?   He crept over as the mound moved once again  and  peered down into the  knee-high  grass . Marcus laughed.   U nder the mound of crystals rose a very familiar  si ght :  the head of a turtle . The man’s eyes were still open and even in death she could see the abject fear on his face. Whatever had done this had scared this man almost to death.  Looking over the other bodies she noticed the same wounds, there were no resin shots or arrows, something had gotten in close and whatever it was, it had some damn sharp claws. Picking up the rifle she checked the chamber and found the round within, in fact none of the guns  were fired. “Whatever did this  come  upon these guys fast, they had no time to pull  their  weapons or fire ,”  she stated as Corliss began walking a circular pattern using the bodies as the  CenterPoint  as she canvased the area for tracks or other items that might point to who did this. Then she found the first set, squatting over the ground Corliss ran her hand over what looked like a bare human foot, except it was just a little too long and she could make out what looked like indents from claws in front of the toes. “What in  Artus ’s  name ? ” she exclaimed calling the other two over. “What do you guys make of this?” she asked and both Burin and  Matest  looked confused as they studied the tracks and the Burin walked a little way finding another set .:  The gate is too long, and look here, hand prints this one was on all fours ,”  he  finished,  and Corliss walked over to join him. Seeing the print, she could also see the quad gouges in the ground “Claws ,”  she whispered, looking back at the bodies as the death scene began to clarify itself in her mind. “Whatever these were, they move too fast, come out of the darkness and were upon them before they realized there was a threat, they held no weapons and using claws strong enough to pierce bronze they cut the soldiers apart ,”  she finished and then reflected on what she had just said.  “We need to go guys, now, if whatever this  was  still out  there,  I damn sure don’t want to meet it ,”  she said and received grunts of agreement from the other two,  the  three got up and began moving back to the  brush line  of the woods “We have movement ,”  one of the elven whispered just loud enough for them to hear. Corliss stopped in her tracks, surveying the direction the elven man was studying. Then she saw it as a splotch of white shot between trees about a hundred yards out. It was too far to make out any detail but whatever it was moved fast she thought, then another further down as bushes moved and she caught another white splotch as it passed by the  brush line .  “We need to move, we do not want to be in the open guys ,”  she  said,  and Corliss turned sprinting back towards the woods, she could hear the footfalls as the two Silvan were on her heals. Then a scream rose from somewhere to  their  left, it curdled her blood as it rose to a  crescendo , another joining it, this one much closer. Cursing silently Corliss willed herself to put on more speed “What are you ? ” she said and finally hit the  brush line  running past the two other wardens as she did. The first Silvan hit the trees and came to stand next to her, but as she watched the last man reached two steps within the  Woodline  and something slammed into it from its right, taking the elven off his feet. Corliss could hear the two seconds of screaming before it ended in a  phlegmy  cough, then nothing.  Without though for herself Corliss burst from the  tree line  to see the shredded body but no attacker, the scream had ended only a moment ago but whatever it was, was already gone. “We need to move  now! ” she screamed, turning and bursting back into the trees. They shot through the woods running as fast as they could, taking a turn around a tree Corliss came up short to find the carcasses of the four horses they had ridden in on laying on the ground where they had left them standing.  They are hunting us .   Scanning overhead for movement, she  crouch ed  down  close to a tree ,  and  slowly she  drew   the mahogany hilt of the straight sword. She could hear the other three fast approaching, putting her arm around the tree she flashed a hand sign and heard when they slowed and then quietly moved to the left and right of her. The tree branches were dark, with no direct moonlight it was next to impossible to see anything, but Corliss continued to slowly scan above. Then she caught movement to her left and looked up to see something skulk along a large  branch, disappearing behind the trunk, it didn’t come out the other side and Corliss frantically looked up and down to see if it had changed elevation instead. As she surveyed the tree her breath caught in her chest as something landed directly to her right. Turning her head slowly she came face to face with the blue glowing eyes of a creature out of nightmares. Cocking its head it studied her, as if curious, it was about the size and shape of a  man,  but its skin was corpse white and its torso was elongated along with its arms and feet, giving it the ability to run on all fours she thought.  The creature stopped cocking its head and went tense for a moment, then with a high screech it reared back to pounce, Corliss shielded her  face,  but nothing hit her, looking over her arm, she saw it laying on the ground an arrow buried deep in its skull, the eyes no longer  glowed,  and the animal man thing just lay there twitching as it gave off its final death throes. The remaining elven appeared from behind a tree further down and walked over to the creature, pulling the arrow from its head and spitting on it. “That is for my brother, demon ,”  he said. They both turned as further down they caught the wail of the other creature she had seen, but this was not a hunting scream, it was a wail of sorrow “It knows we killed its partner ,”  she said and motioned for the others to join her a few moments later another wail floated over the air, but this one came from further away “Its leaving ,”  she finished and realized she had been holding her breath. They waited root there to the spot, watching the trees above like prey animals awaiting the wolf. After a time, they moved, collecting the gear they could carry from the horses and packing the body of the thing the elven had killed and set out for the abbey.  It took most of the night and half the next day before they crested the rise to see the line of soldiers along each side of the ancient abbey. As they walked Corliss to the time to get to know her new ally. “So, I have to ask why  it is  you all look alike, similar the mountain clan they seem to be  their own  species, I have never seen anything like it ,”  she said doing her best not to insult the elven who had saved  their  life. He just smiled giving her a sideways glance. Ages ago the ancient who founded our land had the ability to manipulate genetics with his magic, it was an ability he had cultivated for decades, his abilities and knowledge as a scientist allowed him to take a small group of people and alter them in a way that created our races, there are three us, the dwarfs of the mountain and the  ethereal , though the  ethereal  tend to keep to themselves while the dwarves and Elven keep  steward  over the land. In fact, the ancient named our land after his god ,”  he finished, and Corliss cocked her head curiously, “The ancients god was named Barren ?”   she  asked,  and the Silvan hunter tilted his head back and let out a loud belly laugh. “No, that is what you call our land, its actual name is  Viridi ,”  he finished, and Corliss nodded.  they continued to make their way to the abbey.  By the time they reached the gates, two of the wardens were coming out to meet them on horses. “What happened?” one called down, but Corliss dismissed it, instead handing him the rope to the large sack dragging behind her. “ Get  this into the main building and wait for me ,”  she said, happy to have the heavy bundle  off  her shoulder. Corliss entered the keep finding Uri and  Durras  standing over the bundle and  regarding  it. Uri turned and smiled as she walked through the door “Whatever you brought, smells horrible my dear ,”  he said as Corliss, without a word walked over and motioning the other two to help, hefted the bundle onto the table and unwrapped it.  Once they caught sight of what was under the cloth any joviality in  their  faces quickly washed away. “By  Artus ’s  beard, what is that thing ,”  Uri whispered looking the creature over. Corliss looked at the two men, from the looks on  their  faces neither of them had seen it before and that wasn’t good news. “I was hoping the Silvan had seen this before, but I guess they have not ,”  she said  eliciting  a shrug from  Durras . “I don’t know what it is, but it is fast and deadly, killed a whole squad of  Turin  soldiers before they could get off a shot ,”  she said. “But if none of you have seen it, then  it’s  something new and with everything that has been going on in the territory it means either the Empress or the  mage s have brought new weapons to the field of battle she finished. After they looked it over for nearly thirty minutes,  Durras  called in one of his healers and they left the body with them, while the three of them left the building to walk the perimeter and get some air. Truth be told, no one wanted to be present while the healer cut into the body.  So,  they walked the line checking the defenses and discussing tactics as they did.  After an hour the group returned to find the healer standing outside the building and washing off the blood of the creature. “What can you tell us  Durras  asked her ? ” The healer shook her head and winced at the question. It is like nothing I have ever seen, but I can tell you that it started its life as a normal human, probably was a young lady around seventeen when whatever this is happened to her, she was pregnant as well, but the trauma I am seeing looks as if she had lost the baby during the transformation process, but I can’t be sure ,”  the healer said shaking her head and doing her best to keep the angry and disgusted look off of her face. “Whoever did this to that young girl, is a monster of the worst kind my Lords ,”  she finished the statement hanging in the air between them. “What can you tell us about it, what is the  creatures’  capabilities ? ” Uri  asked,  and the doctor nodded. Some of the bones have been extended and the muscle structure is  changed , this is a creature that is as comfortable running on all  fours  as it is on two legs, it has long sharp and durable claws on its hands for defense and climbing, the claws on the feet look to be only for traction on either a flat surface or aiding it in  ascending . Teeth are sharp, but not long so more for eating then a weapon, however dissecting its corneas the creature can see in low light and normal light, however bright light will probably disorient it for a moment, it looks to have a normal human size brain, but this was buried into it, it wasn’t shoved in ,  but looks to have been surgically implanted ,”  she finished brandishing an odd orange crystal about six inches long. “I don’t know what its purpose is, but whoever inserted used magic to weld it to the cranial bone so it wouldn’t slip out.” With that the doctor bowed to the three men and excused herself.  They watched her go as all three  thoughts  on what the woman had said. Entering the small building they found her assistants cleaning up the table after the dissection.  “So, who do we think made that thing ,”  Corliss asked a shiver ran through her body as she remembered that creature moving through the woods. No one spoke for a moment and finally Uri broke the silence. “We know the Empress has been appointing new Lord Seer’s from the observations these are men with power, either mages that do not report to the order or something new ,”  he  said  and  Durras  turned to  regard  him.  “How do we know they are not part of the order?” he asked though his tone was curious and not challenging so Uri shrugged “Because the tenants the order lives by, don’t kill with magic and every one of these bastards kill the old Lord Seer as an example to the common people of what will happen should they get out of line. That doesn’t sound like the order I know ,”  he  finished  and  Durras  nodded. “Whoever created it, we will need to be vigilant, if the healer’s  assumptions on how it moves are correct, this thing will not be easy to kill ,”  The Silvan General offered as the group went back to reviewing the map. As they reviewed the defenses, making suggestions and notes on changes the front door burst open as an excited initiate came running into the room. “My Lords, a platoon has been seen on the horizon ,”  he yelled with a quick now he rushed out of the room and the three generals followed quickly.  Making their way to the ramparts,  Durras  was the first to arrive, as they gathered Uri pulled out the  farseer —a  tube with the crystals on each end — and began to examine the group of horseback soldiers. “They are  Empress  guard, but what are they doing this far north?” he asked. Corliss cursed silently “They probably found the soldiers from  Turin  and decided to do a patrol to see if there were more, whatever the reason, they have spotted us, now the question is what will they do. “ Durras  squinted looking out over the field “They are too few for an  all-out  assault, but that doesn’t mean they won’t attack,  Warden’s Keep  is only three days ride, they can have backup within the week ,”  he proffered and both men nodded  solemnly  knowing the Silvan general had a point.  Keep the men active and watch them,  let’s  see what they decide to do ,”  Uri said, and the other men nodded in agreement as they turned and headed back into the small building. Before they could leave the ramparts, someone called out and pointed at the small group. Uri looked again and saw the three small carts moving forward, using the  farseer  he examined them and then putting it down handed it to  Durras .  “They look like weapons but nothing I have ever seen before ,”  he  said  and the Elven general took the proffered  farseer , putting his eye to it, he looked out over the field at the odd thing they seemed to be setting it, it was a large metal tube on a wooden cart, the back of it long, as if it were made to lay on the ground as a brace. “The metal tub looks like a short barrel of some kind, is it a new gun, if  so,  they are far back to use it, if the range from the muskets are any indication ,”  he said returning the  farseer  to Uri. “Still,  let’s  have the men take cover as best they can, if this is a weapon, I don’ t  want  to be caught surprised. There have been too many new things we have not seen before to easily dismiss this one , my friend s ,”  he said, and both men nodded.  “Sage advice ,  my Lord  Durras  said as he called two  initiates  over. “Get the men to fall back and take cover, tell them we expect an attack but are unsure of its nature ,”  he finished, and the two initiates scrambled off. It was a mere two hours when they finally discovered the use of  odd - looking carts as they reviewed the area  Durras  setting up two squads of soldiers to perform flanking maneuvers should these soldiers attack a loud boom sounded from across the field, as all three looked up an arc of blue flame shot across the sky coming down just outside the ramparts, the explosion that followed cracked the ancient wall in four places sending mortar and stone flying into the camp. A few screams were heard as a few close to the wall were hit with the stone shrapnel.  “Get back, take cover ! ” Durras  began to yell as he ran towards the wall . H e never quite made it as a second blue arc of flame came down on the inside of the wall ,  and  Durras   w as thrown twenty feet into a line of tents as people began running and screaming, the blue flame blowing outward, like a liquid it splattered on the buildings and stuck there burning.  “Crystal fire ,”  Uri breathed .   “G et everyone as far back as possible ! T hey are using crystal fire ! ”  he yelled, running to aid  Durras  as he began frantically coordinating the men.  Pulling the Silvan general from the collapsed tents, Uri looked him over to find only a few scratches and bruises. “We have to move ,   Durras , ” he  exclaimed ,  a nd  the two of them bolted for the rear of the compound as  Yorst  headed towards the west to direct the troops to take cover. Another salvo of rounds beat into the courtyard of the old abbey as one section of  the  wall collapsed. “We need to take the fight to them ! ”  Yorst  screamed over the raging blue flames ,  and Uri nodded.  Durras  made a motion of his hand ,  and two of the young Silvan nodded gravely  before  taking off.  As the soldiers stood on the hill dialing in the two resin cannons ,  the commander was pleased with the outcome of the new weapons. The Empress’s new innovations have proved incredibly useful so far .  I shall  send her a letter of  compl i ment ,  he thought ,  smiling as another salvo went downrange.  The soldiers, now  de a fened  from the loud report of the cannons, did not hear the whisp of the multitude of arrows as they arced into the encampment ,  and to the commander’s horror ,  almost half the troops collapsed with arrows in  their  backs and chest, as he was about to rally his troops towards the direction of the arrows, another salvo sprang from behind him taking another large swath of his troops, the cannons stood silent as the short dwarven came riding up over the small cover the soldiers had built to cover the cannons and the short horses they rode easily cleared it as the screaming dwarven slaughtered all that was left including the surprised commander who still sat atop his horse trying to figure out what just happened.  An hour later ,  the Silvan troops returned  with  the two cannon s  and a cart of blue crystal resin cannonballs in tow.  Durras  turned to Uri. “If there are more of these, we cannot stay here .   I suggest we ride to Castello ;   it would be the safest place ,”  Durras  stated .   Uri nodded gravely, and  Corliss ,  who stood a short distance away ,  cocked her head .  “The capital of the Silvan people ,”  he said.  It only took four hours to pack everything that  hadn’t  been destroyed,  though  they would have to leave the carts behind .   T he small cannons in tow and tents folded around the blue cannonballs dragged them behind horses as well as supplies and other items too heavy to carry. The entire  procession  made its way into the dense forest of the barrens ,  the wardens leaving the territory of  Vicor  proper for the first time in their history as an organization.  The End
